title: Measles confirmed in 45 states in 2026: CDC data shows kids and teens hit hardest - masslive.com
snippet:
The surge isn’t random — it stems from a series of outbreaks.

The CDC has tracked 35 new outbreaks this year. An outbreak is considered a cluster of three or more cases in a given community.

In 2026, a staggering 93% of all cases trace back to a single outbreak.

Patients who were unvaccinated accounted for 93% of the cases — matching last year’s trend.

## The one bright spot

Fewer patients infected with measles are ending up hospitalized this year compared with previous years. [...] As of July 24 measles has confirmed cases in 45 states and jurisdictions — plus D.C. — with 16 more among international visitors, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data shows.

## Kids and teens are bearing the brunt

About 7 in 10 measles cases are in people under 20, and nearly half of all cases are kids aged 5 to 19 — a bigger share than last year.

Toddlers under 5 make up a smaller slice though — accounting for 20% of all cases compared to 26% in 2025.

## Measles outbreaks [...] In 2026, 7% of people with the virus — 151 people — were hospitalized.

That’s down from 11% last year. The drop was steepest among kids under 5, whose hospitalization rate nearly halved from 18% to 10%.

As of July 2026, there have been zero measles deaths in the U.S. versus three in 2025.

## Why is this happening?

CDC data points to a drop in vaccination rates alongside the hike in measles cases.

The UKHSA said one child died from “acute measles” and another child’s death was linked to the “late effects of measles”. This is compared to 959 cases for the whole of 2025.

The majority (449 out of 736, 61%) were in unvaccinated children aged 10 years and under, and 34% (247 out of 736) were in young people and adults aged 15 years and over.

title: Measles Cases Are On the Rise Globally: What It Means for Children
snippet:
Over the past five years, measles outbreaks have hit more than 100 countries. Canada lost its official measles elimination status on Nov. 10, 2025. The United States could be next as measles cases in the U.S. continue to rise. [...] On July 7, 2025, the U.S. passed a sobering milestone: the number of measles cases across the country reached its highest point in three decades, with 1,281 cases reported — the most since the highly contagious disease was officially eliminated in the U.S. back in 2000. And the year was only half over. As of Nov. 4, that total had risen to 1,681 confirmed cases, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). [...] Both the U.S. and Mexico have had sustained measles outbreaks since early 2025, putting them on track to lose their measles-free status in 2026.

## As measles cases surge, here are five things to know:

### 1. Measles can be deadly.

Measles kills nearly 300 people every day, approximately 12 people every hour, mostly children under 5. Even when children survive a measles infection, the virus can leave them with long-term health effects or permanent disabilities.

Maintaining high vaccination coverage remains the most cost-effective means of preventing outbreaks and protecting public health investments — not just for measles but for many diseases of public health concern. As vaccination rates decline in some areas of the United States and outbreaks continue to rise in 2026, understanding the cost of a response is increasingly important for public health officials, legislators, and other decision-makers. [...] Ultimately, these cost estimates combined with accurate information on vaccine safety and the health risks of measles (and other infections) can mobilize policymakers and the public to increase and sustain vaccination coverage in their communities.
